correctness.rationale: All k>=2 and all gap lists with at least one long gap are covered. The k one-ending arches prove k-universality, pigeonhole and adjacent-pair embeddings classify length k+1 absences, internal double-gap cuts have exactly one missing pattern by a proved greedy estimate, reverse cuts preserve the count, and short-gap terminal streaks partition all remaining cuts. Fibonacci morphism and coprime counts establish its specialization and primitivity. Independent Python brute enumerations of 501 gap lists/8890 cuts plus DP Fibonacci levels 3..11 succeeded; finite checks are corroboration, not infinite proof.

originality.rationale: Compared exact cyclic run-length histogram and Fibonacci conjugacy multiplicities, including prior stronger abstract tools, rather than relying on title similarity. The close 2021 and 2022 sources count absent subsequences for an individual linear word and the 2022 paper has an algorithmic general characterization; neither states the cyclic distribution or the Fibonacci specialization. A closed orbit formula requires proof of how cuts and terminal short-gap streaks interact. Searches of prior published findings and related literature revealed no equivalent; earlier unindexed equivalent result remains possible.
residual_risks: An unindexed earlier paper or database could contain an equivalent cyclic-gap formula.

The 2022 general nearly-universal word counting construction covers the problem algorithmically and could yield this result after nontrivial specialization; this work only claims novelty of the explicit cyclic and Fibonacci classifications.
No independent literature audit has been performed.

value.rationale: Provides a complete exact finite-valued invariant across an infinite natural family of circular binary words, parameterized by run lengths of short gaps rather than cyclic order, and yields all Fibonacci substitution levels with explicit distinct-rotation multiplicities. This solves a motivated whole-neighborhood combinatorial classification, not an arbitrary small computation.
